title: Python dead code: what 51 popular Python repos ship that nothing imports
summary:
TL;DR

  • 45 of 50 popular Python repos (1,000+ GitHub stars) have at least one dead-code finding in production code, and in the median repo 3.9% of production files are flagged as unreachable.
  • In Python, a file nothing imports is often loaded by name: 82 of Django's 100 dead-code candidates are locale files imported from a string at runtime.
  • 814 of the 819 files flagged in LangChain are compatibility shims that keep old import paths working for its users.

title: Flutter BLoC: Building a Feature with Events, States, and Cubit
summary:
Series 4 — Part 1 of 1

Flutter BLoC: Building a Feature with Events, States, and Cubit

A standalone deep-dive on the BLoC pattern in Flutter

After GetX, my next exploration was Flutter BLoC — the pattern that treats UI as a function of state, and models every user action as an explicit event. BLoC is more verbose than either Riverpod or GetX, but it is also the most explicit about intent.

I spent two days reading the official BLoC documentation, watching walkthroughs, and building a basic implementation with MVVM architecture.

The BLoC mental model

BLoC stands for Business Logic Component. The pattern works like this: the UI emits Events, the BLoC processes them and emits new States, and the UI rebuilds based on the current State. Nothing is hidden. Every transition is traceable.

title: 0.1 + 0.2 Is Not a Bug. It's Arithmetic in a Costume.
summary:
The first time 0.30000000000000004 showed up on my screen I did what everyone does. I blamed Python. Then I blamed my keyboard. Then Python again, louder.

It's not Python. JavaScript prints the same number, and so does nearly every language on your machine, because nearly every language stores decimals the same way: as IEEE 754 doubles, a standard from 1985 that is older than most of the people complaining about it.

Where does the extra 4 come from?

Write one third as a decimal. You can't. You get 0.333 and then the 3s keep going until you run out of patience or paper, and whatever you eventually write down is close to a third but is not a third.

Binary has the same problem with different numbers. 0.1 in binary is 0.0001100110011..., the "0011" repeating forever. A double gives you 53 bits of precision to store that with, so the machine stores the closest value it can fit and moves on.

title: Long-horizon agents and durable execution
summary: Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior. Kiran Prakash explains durable execution: an emerging pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards their goal. In this programming model, the runtime keeps a record of the result of each step that interacts with the outside world so that, when a failure occurs, the program runs again, completed steps are skipped, and the program's state is rebuilt from the record.

title: In the Hole
summary:
Look, I don't want to keep talking about security issues. Blame AI. Just another thing it ruined.

At this point, you've probably heard about *sshole. If you haven't, the quick summary: on some Linux systems, SSH will log you in to an account with no password if you supply a password greater than 256 characters long. Frequently, you might make accounts like root nominally inaccessible by giving it no password, so this is a big deal. Worse, it impacts varieties of Linux that use the musl implementation of libc, like Alpine- the kinds of varieties that run inside a container hosting a web app somewhere.

The impact is broad, and is definitely being exploited. The root cause, however, is interesting, because it's a sum of very simple choices that lead to a wildly undesirable result.
